title: JUST DOWN THE ROAD A PIECE The Development of Topological Knowledge of Building Layouts
research_question: Does people's topological knowledge of a setting change as they become more familiar with it, specifically shifting from reliance on local to more global topological qualities?

participants.description: 62 male and 66 female students, mostly aged 17 to 25 (mean = 19.5), from a major U.S. city. Screened to have visited a large hospital no more than once in the prior 12 months.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three large, complex urban hospitals: Urban Hospital, University Hospital, and City Hospital. Each hospital had preselected entry points and four specific locations (1-4) used as origins and destinations for directed searches.

mechanisms: People learn about the environment sequentially as they move through it, processing successive input into a comprehensive understanding.

In initial stages of exploration, people rely on local topological qualities (e.g., connectivity, DP degree, nodes recognized) that offer a better sense of other spaces through visual connections and possibilities for exploration.

As familiarity increases, cognitive understanding progresses from local to more global topological properties (e.g., actual node integration), allowing reliance on a broader understanding of the configuration.
Configuration creates movement, which in turn promotes an understanding of the configurational properties, contributing to more accurate movement and wayfinding.
moderators: Familiarity with the setting (new users vs. experienced users)
Task type (open exploration vs. directed search)
implementation_implications: Space syntax analysis can be a good tool for testing possible wayfinding difficulties in complex buildings and projects.
Considering the role of local and relational qualities (e.g., connectivity for new users) can help fine-tune wayfinding design methods.

limitations: The study was conducted in three large urban hospitals, which may not generalize to other building types or environments.
Participants were students aged 17-25, potentially limiting generalizability to other age groups or populations.
The time gap for learning (10-15 minutes) might be specific to the experimental conditions and not reflect real-world learning rates.

paper_metadata.title: Just Down The Road A Piece
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Just Down The Road A Piece
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This study explores whether people’s topological knowledge changes as they get to know a setting. Volunteers ( n = 128) performed open and directed searches in three large hospitals. In open searches the participants attempted to become familiar with the hospital; in directed searches they sought specific locations. The participants also performed various cognitive tasks such as pointing and sketch mapping. During initial exploration, they relied more on local topological qualities, such as how many additional nodal decision points could be seen from a given node. As they got to know the setting better, their wayfinding behavior was better predicted by more global qualities such as the space syntax integration of a node. This suggests that people rapidly move from a local to a more global topological understanding as they learn a setting. In addition, space syntax measures were good predictors of the participant's ability to point to out-of-sight locations and of their sketch maps.
